title: Ukraine Launches Its Largest Drone Attack on Moscow, Striking a Key Oil Refinery, as Merz's CDU Slumps Below 5% in German State Votes
subhead: Kyiv fired hundreds of drones at the Russian capital in the biggest such assault of the war, hitting a refinery that supplies a third of Moscow's fuel, even as Moscow held tightly controlled parliamentary elections. In Germany, Chancellor Merz's party suffered state-election losses that left him fighting to keep his job.

sections.heading: Largest Drone Barrage on Moscow Hits Fuel Supply
sections.body:
Ukraine launched its largest drone attack on the Moscow region since the war began, Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said, with 450 drones heading for the capital shot down overnight. The regional governor said at least two people were killed and 20 injured. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed Kyiv had hit a 'key' Russian oil facility and a logistics site in the region with drones and missiles, facilities he said represent 'billions of dollars that sustain the war machine'. The refinery struck supplies more than a third of the Moscow region's fuel, according to Kyiv's defence ministry, and part of its petrol, diesel and aviation fuel goes to Russia's military. Ukrainian military officials said three key units at the plant were damaged, and major airports including Sheremetyevo and Vnukovo imposed flight restrictions, with Vnukovo briefly halting all arrivals and departures.

The assault on Sunday landed on the third day of Russia's parliamentary election, which is tightly controlled by the Kremlin. Sobyanin described the attack as an attempt to disrupt the vote. Ukrainian officials, meanwhile, said nine people including three children were killed in Russian strikes on the Kyiv and Sumy regions on Saturday, underlining how both sides have intensified attacks on energy, transport and logistics targets. BBC reports the drone strike was the most massive to hit the capital region, with videos verified by the broadcaster showing explosions in the night sky above Moscow.
sections.whyItMatters: A strike this large on the capital's fuel infrastructure, timed to Russia's elections, shows Ukraine's growing reach and willingness to target the economic underpinnings of Russia's war effort — a qualitative step in the air campaign that Moscow's air defences could not fully stop.

sections.heading: Merz's CDU Suffers State-Election Disaster, AfD Gains
sections.body:
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz called the result 'a disaster' for his party after exit polls showed the Christian Democratic Union (CDU) slumped below the 5 percent threshold needed to stay in parliament in the north-eastern state of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern — its worst result there ever, according to projections reported by the BBC. In Berlin, the CDU-led government was expected to be beaten by Die Linke (The Left). The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) was on track to win the most votes in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, though it is unlikely to govern as other parties refuse to work with it. AfD co-leader Alice Weidel said the party had 'reached the mainstream of the population'.

Merz, under mounting pressure with poor approval ratings and speculation about a mid-term 'chancellor swap', vowed to stay on and push forward his coalition's package of economic, tax and welfare reforms. 'The reforms have to come,' Merz told reporters at the party's Berlin headquarters, calling them 'the antidote to the authoritarian poison'. Some branches of the AfD are classed as right-wing extremist by domestic intelligence, a designation the party rejects, but its anti-immigration, German-first and Russian-friendly agenda has found fertile ground in the former communist east, the BBC notes.
sections.whyItMatters: A chancellor falling below the threshold in a state vote and facing speculation of replacement signals deep fragility at the heart of Europe's largest economy, while the AfD's advance reshapes the political balance in the east ahead of the 2027 federal election.

sections.heading: Pakistan Detains Imran Khan's Sister Ahead of National Protests
sections.body:
Aleema Khanum, the sister of Pakistan's imprisoned former prime minister Imran Khan, was arrested in Lahore on Sunday afternoon, her Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party said, describing it as an 'illegal detention'. The arrest order, issued by Lahore's deputy commissioner, alleged she was mobilising Khan's supporters 'through social media and public meetings' and accused her of encouraging people to 'create law and order situations', according to the BBC. Her son Shahrez Khan demanded the government 'disclose her whereabouts and ensure her safe return'. A police official confirmed the arrest, and the order says she will be held for 30 days at Kot Lakhpat jail.

Many observers link the detention to protests organised for 27 September, when demonstrators plan to march on the capital, Islamabad. Streets in the capital are already lined with shipping containers to safeguard government buildings, the BBC reports. Khanum, a vocal critic of her brother's detention, had regularly addressed his supporters and the media.
sections.whyItMatters: Detaining a senior opposition figure days before planned marches is an escalation in the pressure campaign against Khan's movement, raising the stakes for the 27 September protest and the stability of the civilian government in a nuclear-armed state.

sections.heading: Iran War Reshapes Global Fuel Trade as South Korea Rides to Europe's Rescue
sections.body:
Europe faces a fourth-quarter jet fuel deficit of 510,000 barrels per day, consultancy Energy Aspects forecasts, with the continent turning to far-flung suppliers after the six-month-old Iran war cut off roughly half of its jet imports, according to the South China Morning Post. South Korea has become the latest large source of supply, boosting jet exports to Europe to a four-year high in September at 129,000 barrels per day, per Kpler shipping data, with LSEG showing similar volumes. Europe has also been importing more jet fuel from Nigeria, the United States and Canada since the escalation began.

The disruption stems from a conflict that continues to shape global markets and strategy. In the Gulf, the Houthis said they targeted Saudi Arabia's capital Riyadh with ballistic missiles, with a reported strike on a fuel depot at Riyadh airport causing delays on Saturday, while Saudi Arabia said it shot down a missile aimed at the capital, the BBC reported. Al Jazeera notes Tehran has also pushed a mass mobilisation drive — the Janfada or 'those who sacrifice their life' campaign, run through the Basij militia arm of the IRGC — training volunteer civilians, with recruits holding a first public 'military exercise' in Tehran on Friday.
sections.whyItMatters: The ongoing Iran conflict is not just a military story — it is rerouting global energy supply chains, forcing Europe to import jet fuel from Asia and the Americas at record distances, a reminder of the durable economic cost that outlasts any single headline.

bottomLine: Today's defining development was Ukraine's largest drone assault on Moscow, which hit a refinery feeding a third of the capital's fuel supply during Russia's election — a tangible escalation in economic warfare that Moscow's defences could not fully contain. At the same time, Germany's chancellor stumbled in state elections with the far-right surging, Pakistan moved against Imran Khan's family ahead of nationwide protests, and the Iran war kept redrawing global fuel routes. The takeaway: the fighting in Ukraine and the Middle East continues to generate new strategic shocks, even as domestic politics in major European powers grows more volatile.
